children: Iron ore prices fell for a third straight session on Friday and were heading for their first weekly loss in three, pressured by lower-than-anticipated demand and a sharp squeeze in steel margins in top consumer China.
The most-traded iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
closed daytime trade down 1.78% at 718 yuan ($107.03) a metric ton, its lowest level since September 3. It logged a drop of 1.1% through Friday, the biggest weekly decline since late July.

Benchmark October iron ore (SZZFV6) on the Singapore Exchange slid 1.47% to $96.75 a ton as of 0700 GMT, on track for a decline of about 3% so far this week, the biggest weekly fall in nearly three months.
Demand for the key steelmaking ingredient fell as some steelmakers trimmed output amid widening losses.

Average daily hot metal output in China, a gauge of iron ore demand, dipped by 0.2% from the week before to 2.36 million tons as of September 10, while only around 7.8% of steelmakers were operating at a profit, compared to 30% the week before, data from consultancy Mysteel showed.

"China is unlikely to drive another structural supercycle," analysts at BMI said in a note, seeing $80 a ton as an increasingly meaningful level of support. They also suggested the Simandou iron ore project in Guinea, which is ramping up supply along with other sources of supply growth, should constrain prices over time.
